title: Department of War Daily Briefing
description: Secretary-level initiatives, acquisition, Golden Dome, operations and policy across the Department of War.
readFirst: Covers Oct. 22–30. New: Military.com reported Oct. 30 that a Defense Department spokesperson said Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia's firing was for severe misconduct and that he was not the Iran war's central planner, and Federal News Network reported Oct. 29 that movers are pushing back on proposed CMMC Level 2 rules for household-goods moves. No new Golden Dome appropriation was found. The Department of War site did not return an Oct. 30 readout of the Sylvia removal.

items.headline: Hegseth fired J5 Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia; a spokesperson says he was not the Iran war planner
items.summary: Military.com reported Oct. 30 that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff director for strategy, plans and policy, on Thursday. Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed the firing on X and wrote that the Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information. A department spokesperson told Military.com the termination was for severe misconduct, that Sylvia was not a central planner for the Iran war, that the central planner is CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper, and that Sylvia is under investigation for leaking classified information about the Iran war, the Russia-Ukraine war, and more, including by meeting journalists outside the Pentagon after an escort rule. CBS News reported Oct. 29 that an official said Sylvia failed three polygraph tests and that the case was referred to the Justice Department, and NBC News reported the Pentagon first thanked Sylvia for his service and rescinded that statement a day later.

items.headline: In Cebu, Hegseth tells ASEAN defense ministers the U.S. line is strong, quiet, and clear
items.summary: The Diplomat reported Oct. 29 that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth told the ASEAN Defense Ministers' Meeting in Cebu on Oct. 28 that the U.S. approach is strong, quiet, and clear, and that the United States will defend its interests and those of its allies and partners. Hegseth said Washington would back that with practical cooperation, including maritime domain awareness, interoperability, and cooperation among navies. He proposed a U.S.-ASEAN Framework for Defense Cooperation and did not give further details of the pact. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said a robust U.S. presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and the broader Indo-Pacific.

items.headline: In Cebu, Hegseth and Japan's defense minister agree on cyber cooperation and a First Island Chain denial defense
items.summary: The Japan Times reported Oct. 28 that Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth met in Cebu on the sidelines of the ASEAN defense ministers' meeting and agreed to strengthen cooperation against cyberattacks. Japan's Defense Ministry said the two agreed to keep coordinating so malicious cyber activity, including large-scale leaks of personal information, does not seriously affect daily life, economic activity, or the security of both countries. Nippon.com, citing a U.S. Defense Department announcement, reported that the two underscored more defense investment and strategic alignment for an effective denial defense in the First Island Chain, and that they agreed to work closely on ammunition production. The Tribune reported the same day that Indian Defence Minister Rajnath Singh met Hegseth in Cebu, and that Hegseth said they marked one year of the Framework for the U.S.-India Major Defense Partnership.

items.headline: Hegseth bars troops and civilians from using nonpublic information to bet on military operations
items.summary: DefenseScoop reported Oct. 22 that it obtained an Oct. 20 memorandum in which Secretary of War Pete Hegseth barred Pentagon and military personnel from placing financial wagers, including on Polymarket or Kalshi, using nonpublic government information. The memo says the prohibition applies to classified or unclassified information, and that violations may bring administrative, disciplinary, or criminal action under the Uniform Code of Military Justice or federal law. Hegseth wrote that enemies watch these markets and that a transaction on a military outcome creates a signal. Stars and Stripes reported Oct. 23 that the order also covers indirect bets through third parties, and that prosecutors allege Army Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who pleaded not guilty, won more than $400,000 on Polymarket using classified information about the January operation that captured Nicolas Maduro.

items.headline: Federal News Network: movers ask DoD to drop CMMC Level 2 from household-goods rules
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Oct. 29 that Movers for America is urging the Defense Department to revise proposed rules for the Defense Personal Property program, and that public comments closed Oct. 26. Executive director Katie McMichael told Federal News Network that CMMC Level 2 is very costly for an industry of small businesses and independent contractors, and that the group does not think CMMC is necessary for the names, addresses, and phone numbers movers receive. She said a Movers for America survey found nearly half of moving professionals might scale back Defense Department business if Level 2 is required. The outlet says the proposed rules would prohibit service members from sponsoring or escorting movers onto installations, and that the Personal Property Activity is expected to release final rules by the end of November.

items.headline: Pentagon contracting staff get templates for buying AI the department calls unbiased
items.summary: Federal News Network reported Oct. 26 that John Tenaglia, principal director for defense pricing, contracting and acquisition policy, issued guidance so artificial intelligence the department buys follows what the administration calls truth-seeking and ideological neutrality. Tenaglia wrote that compliance with a July executive order and a later Office of Management and Budget memo is mandatory, and that the Pentagon document is guidance only so components can tailor the language. Federal News Network says the templates include a memo for choosing transparency and documentation requirements, standardized solicitation language, and contract language for a statement of work or performance work statement. The story ties the memo to Secretary Hegseth's push to field commercial AI, including compute from data centers to the tactical edge.

items.headline: Project Agincourt's West and Strasiser say Autonomous Warfare Command is due Oct. 1, 2027
items.summary: The Department of War reported Oct. 23 that Owen West and Max Strasiser, identified as chief executive and chief operating officer of Project Agincourt and appointed by Secretary Hegseth, sent an open letter on how the Autonomous Warfare Command will develop. The story says Hegseth tasked them with standing up the four-star functional combatant command and with continuing the direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems. They wrote that the Cold War model of a small number of sophisticated, expensive weapons has been disrupted, and that an advantage now depends on adapting at the edge with a lead in super intelligence and the noncommissioned officer corps. The command is expected to be operational by Oct. 1, 2027, and they said success is how fast an operational problem receives a fielded, scalable solution.

items.headline: AUKUS: USS Colorado is the first U.S. submarine named for Submarine Rotational Force-West
items.summary: The Department of War said Oct. 26 that Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Australian Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Richard Marles, and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting designated USS Colorado (SSN 788) as the first U.S. Navy Virginia-class fast-attack submarine assigned to Submarine Rotational Force-West, beginning in late 2027. The release says the force is projected to host up to four U.S. fast-attack submarines and one UK fast-attack submarine on a rotational basis at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia. It says a U.S. submarine maintenance period begins later this week to show Australia's ability to sustain U.S. and UK nuclear-powered attack submarines. The statement says the move is an AUKUS Pillar I milestone and that the partners describe AUKUS as moving full steam ahead.

items.headline: Fox: FORTRESS documents would have major U.S. bases last 90 days without outside support
items.summary: Fox News Digital reported Oct. 25, citing documents it reviewed, that under an initiative called FORTRESS every major military installation in the continental United States would be expected to sustain essential operations independently for at least 90 days, including electricity, water, fuel and communications. Pentagon chief spokesperson Sean Parnell, who Fox said led the initiative, told Fox that power is combat now and that without electricity the department loses communications, water, logistics, assembly lines and basic command structures. Fox says the documents envision portable nuclear reactors, large-scale battery storage and microgrids that can disconnect bases from the civilian grid, plus reserves of munitions, fuel, critical minerals, electronics, spare parts and medical supplies. Fox also says the most critical dependencies would need at least two qualified supply or production pathways, and that the Civil Reserve Manufacturing Network is folded into FORTRESS so commercial factories can be identified to shift to defense production.

items.headline: CENTCOM: U.S. forces helped Gulf partners export more than 1.5 billion barrels through Hormuz
items.summary: CENTCOM said Oct. 25 that Adm. Brad Cooper visited the Strait of Hormuz as U.S. forces reached a milestone of assisting Gulf partners in exporting more than 1.5 billion barrels of crude oil since summer. Cooper observed traffic from a U.S. Army CH-47 Chinook with Maj. Gen. Brandon Tegtmeier, commander of the 82nd Airborne Division. CENTCOM said more than 3,000 commercial vessels have transited the strait with its support over the last six months, and that primary transit routes remain free of Iranian sea mines. It said that in recent months more than 95 percent of ships navigating the strait have sailed through safely.
